title: Sunni and Shia Traditions
welcome_lead: Explore the rich Sunni and Shia traditions arising after the Prophet's death in 632 CE.

final_note: You have approached the Sunni and Shia traditions with care. Both share the Qur'an and the Prophet.

Branch of Islam (about 10-13%) holding that leadership belonged to Ali and his descendants.
Shia doctrine of divinely guided successors of the Prophet, central to Shia identity.

walkthroughs.body_html: After the Prophet's death in 632 CE, the community split over succession. Sunni Muslims accepted Abu Bakr as first caliph, followed by Umar, Uthman and Ali. Shia Muslims regarded Ali, the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, as the rightful successor and rejected the first three caliphs' authority.

Shia Muslims commemorate the martyrdom of Husayn at Karbala (680 CE) during Ashura. They emphasise the imamate; Twelvers await the return of the hidden imam (the Mahdi). Sunni and Shia share core beliefs, the Qur'an, fasting in Ramadan and Hajj, while differing on certain laws and rituals.

Hajj takes place in the lunar month of Dhu al-Hijjah. Pilgrims perform tawaf around the Kaaba, sa'i between Safa and Marwah, the standing at Arafat, the symbolic stoning at Mina and animal sacrifice during Eid al-Adha. Around 2 million pilgrims attend annually in recent years.

mcqs.q: What does the teleological (design) argument claim?
options: Apparent purpose, order or complexity in the universe implies an intelligent designer — Paley's watchmaker analogy is the classic example.
The design argument proves evolution is false.
Buddhism teaches that suffering is caused by demons.
The design argument proves God created the world in seven days.
